```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>",
                      fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4)
```

This vignette walks through a typical GeoModelR session using the primate
example data shipped with the package: one dated primate phylogeny (894
species, living and fossil) and a short excerpt (50 posterior samples) of a
BayesTraits Geo model run from Avaria-Llautureo et al. (2025).

The workflow has three parts:

1. **Before BayesTraits** - clean the input coordinates and prepare
   palaeomaps.
2. **Run BayesTraits** - the Geo model itself (outside R).
3. **After BayesTraits** - read the output, map ancestral locations and
   measure dispersal.

Chunks that need the GPlates Web Service (internet) are shown but not run
here.

```{r}
library(GeoModelR)
```

## 1. Example data

```{r}
anc_file  <- system.file("extdata", "Primate.AncStates.txt", package = "GeoModelR")
tree_file <- system.file("extdata", "Median.trees", package = "GeoModelR")

phy <- ape::read.nexus(tree_file)
phy
```

## 2. Before BayesTraits

### Clean sister-taxon coordinates

Under the variable-rates Geo model, sister taxa whose input coordinates are
less than about 50 m apart can have the branches between them compressed to
zero length. `clean_sister_geodata()` checks every pair of sister tips (and,
optionally, a tip against its sister cherry) and removes overlapping
distribution points.

The two BayesTraits input files are usually read like this:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
single <- read.table("Single_Coord_Data.txt", sep = "\t", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
dist   <- read.table("Distribution_Data.txt", sep = "\t", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
```

Here is a small made-up example so that every case appears:

```{r}
toy <- ape::read.tree(text = "((A:1,B:1):1,(C:1,(D:1,E:1):1):1);")

single <- data.frame(V1 = c("A", "B", "C", "D", "E"),
                     V2 = c(-70, -70.0002, -60, 10, 10.2),   # A and B ~20 m apart
                     V3 = c(-30, -30, -20, 45, 45.2))

dist <- data.frame(V1 = c("D", "E"), V2 = "Linked",
                   V3 = c("10,10.5,11", "10.00001,12"),        # one shared point
                   V4 = c("45,45.5,46", "45,47"))
```

When two sisters both rely on a single centroid and those centroids
overlap, the function does not guess. It stops and lists the pairs:

```{r, error = TRUE}
clean_sister_geodata(toy, single, dist)
```

You decide which taxon to remove (or correct its coordinates) and run it
again. The taxon is removed from the data and from the tree:

```{r}
res <- clean_sister_geodata(toy, single, dist, delete = "B")
```

The shared point was deleted from D, the taxon with more distribution
points:

```{r}
res$deletion_log
res$clean_distdata
```

In an interactive session, `ask = TRUE` shows a menu for each conflict
instead. Write the cleaned files and tree for BayesTraits with:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
write.table(res$clean_singledata, "Single_Coord_Data_clean.txt", sep = "\t",
            row.names = FALSE, col.names = FALSE, quote = FALSE)
write.table(res$clean_distdata, "Distribution_Data_clean.txt", sep = "\t",
            row.names = FALSE, col.names = FALSE, quote = FALSE)
ape::write.nexus(res$clean_tree, file = "tree_clean.nex")
```

### Prepare palaeomaps

Download one palaeocoastline map per million years, convert them to the
land/ocean grids BayesTraits reads, and write the `BuildMaps` file:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
max_age <- ceiling(max(ape::node.depth.edgelength(phy)))
maps <- get_paleomaps(max_age = max_age, model = "PALEOMAP")
maps <- fill_missing_maps(maps)          # retry any ages that failed

sf_to_csv(age = maps$ages, maps = maps, resolution = 1, dir = "maps_csv")
write_buildmaps_file(maps, bin_file = "PrimateMaps.bin",
                     out_file = "BuildPrimateMaps.txt")
```

Then, in BayesTraits, `BuildMaps BuildPrimateMaps.txt` and
`LoadMaps PrimateMaps.bin`.

## 3. After BayesTraits

### Read the output

`read_geo_ancstates()` parses the `*.AncStates.txt` file. Supplying the tree
adds an `ape_node` column, so nodes can be referred to by their BayesTraits
name or their ape number. The tree must be the one used in the analysis:
`add_ape_nodes()` stops if any clade does not match exactly.

```{r}
geo <- read_geo_ancstates(anc_file, phy = phy)
geo
```

`geo$coords` holds one row per node and posterior sample:

```{r}
head(geo$coords[, c("node_name", "ape_node", "iteration",
                    "longitude", "latitude", "height")])
```

### Summarise a node

The crown primate node is the most recent common ancestor of a lemur and
a human:

```{r}
crown <- ape::getMRCA(phy, c("Lemur_catta", "Homo_sapiens"))
crown_nm <- geo$nodes$node_name[geo$nodes$ape_node == crown]
crown_nm

s <- geo$coords[geo$coords$node_name == crown_nm, ]
c(age_Ma = unique(s$height),
  median_lon = median(s$longitude),
  median_lat = median(s$latitude))
```

### Map ancestral locations

The plotting functions draw the posterior samples on the palaeomap of each
node's age. They download maps, so they are not run here. Download the maps
once with `get_paleomaps()` and pass them via `maps` to avoid repeated
requests.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
maps <- get_paleomaps(geo)

plot_node(geo, crown_nm, maps = maps, show_density = TRUE)
plot_node(geo, crown_nm, phy = phy, maps = maps)          # with tree panel

plot_timeinterval(geo, age_min = 50, age_max = 56, maps = maps)

lemurs <- find_tips(geo, "^(Lemur|Eulemur|Varecia)_")
plot_clade(geo, tips = lemurs, maps = maps)
```

### Dispersal distances

`get_dispersal_distance()` measures great-circle distances between parent
and child nodes for every branch and posterior sample (`type = "branch"`),
or cumulative root-to-tip distances (`type = "path"`).

```{r}
bd <- get_dispersal_distance(geo, phy, type = "branch", nodes = "tips")
bd$rate_km_per_myr <- bd$distance_km / bd$branch_time_myr
head(bd[, c("tip_label", "iteration", "distance_km", "branch_time_myr",
            "rate_km_per_myr")])
```

Posterior median terminal-branch distance per species:

```{r}
med <- aggregate(distance_km ~ tip_label, data = bd, FUN = median)
head(med[order(-med$distance_km), ], 5)
```

Cumulative distance travelled by each lineage against its age:

```{r}
pd <- get_dispersal_distance(geo, phy, type = "path")
pd_med <- aggregate(cbind(path_distance_km, lineage_time_myr) ~ tip_label,
                    data = pd, FUN = median)

library(ggplot2)
ggplot(pd_med, aes(lineage_time_myr, path_distance_km / 1000)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  labs(x = "Time since the root (Myr)",
       y = "Root-to-tip distance (1000 km)") +
  theme_bw()
```

### Palaeo frame vs plate frame

By default (`frame = "palaeo"`) distances are measured between the
palaeocoordinates as sampled, following O'Donovan et al. (2018) and
Avaria-Llautureo et al. (2025). These include the movement of the plates
that carried each lineage. With `frame = "plate"`, each node's samples are
first reconstructed to their present-day position on their plate, which
removes plate motion. Samples that cannot be reconstructed are kept with
`NA` distances and counted per node:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
bd_plate <- get_dispersal_distance(geo, phy, frame = "plate")
attr(bd_plate, "reconstruction")
```

## References

Avaria-Llautureo, J., Püschel, T. A., Meade, A., Baker, J., Nicholson, S. L.,
& Venditti, C. (2025). The radiation and geographic expansion of primates
through diverse climates. *PNAS*, 122(32), e2423833122.
<https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2423833122>

O'Donovan, C., Meade, A., & Venditti, C. (2018). Dinosaurs reveal the
geographical signature of an evolutionary radiation. *Nature Ecology &
Evolution*, 2, 452-458. <https://doi.org/10.1038/s41559-017-0454-6>
